clue.text: Eagerness to get things for grasping Head

parts.note: grasping in the sense of greedy, keen to acquire
a ness is a headland, as in Orford Ness on the Suffolk coast

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss on greed, saying it is the quality of a grasping mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Head looks like a person in charge, but it is a geographical headland; NESS ends many British coastal place names.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the quality of being keen to acquire possessions, which is what eagerness to get things describes.

clue.text: Move chair and find spider

indicators.note: to move things is to shift them about, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Shift a piece of furniture and discover a spider lurking underneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is one example of the class of eight-legged creatures, so the class name stands for it here.

clue.text: Time to be penitent? Correct

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
to rue is to regret or repent

explanation.surface: A question about whether this is the moment for repentance, answered with a confident yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something correct is accurate, which is a plain synonym for the answer as an adjective.

clue.text: Levelling with old Bob when the sun goes down

parts.note: evening a surface means levelling it
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Someone smoothing ground with an elderly helper named Bob as dusk falls.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob is not a name: it is slang for the pre-decimal British shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Evenings are the times of day around sunset, so the phrase describing sundown stands for them.

clue.text: Toy with a little dessert
ET dined when set apart

parts.note: ET is the extraterrestrial of the Spielberg film
past tense of eat

explanation.surface: The film's extraterrestrial took his meal away from everybody else.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate or estrange someone from others is to set them apart, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Skilled in some ways, but served criminal

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or wrong, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crook who is talented in certain respects has nonetheless done time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served' suggests a prison sentence; it is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Being versed in a subject means being knowledgeable or practised in it, hence skilled in particular areas.

clue.text: Banded in error at mealtime, guests come to terms

definitions.note: a descriptive definition: the lodging deal guests agree to

indicators.note: letters set down in error are in the wrong order and must be put right

parts.note: the six letters of this word, rearranged
the first mealtime of the day

explanation.surface: Diners wrongly grouped at a meal manage to reach an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to terms' sounds like reconciling; the terms are the room-and-morning-meal deal a guesthouse offers.
explanation.definitionFit: A guesthouse arrangement offering a room overnight and a morning meal is the set of terms its guests accept.

clue.text: Joker with flower for motorist

parts.note: a card is a joker, a funny person (and the joker is a playing card)
a flower is something that flows, a crossword favourite for a river; 'with' joins it on

explanation.surface: A comedian bearing a bunch of blooms as a present for someone at the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is read as flow-er, a thing that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist is anyone who drives a car, so the two terms are synonyms.

clue.text: Belgian town faithful to a lord in the Middle Ages

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the city in eastern Belgium

definitions.text: faithful to a lord in the Middle Ages
definitions.meaning: second meaning: owing feudal allegiance to an overlord

explanation.walkthrough: The Belgian city and the feudal adjective share their spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal society a vassal was bound in loyalty to his overlord, the medieval sense of this adjective.

clue.text: Foul article on uncle

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is placed after it, so the article comes second

parts.note: taken as written
an indefinite article

explanation.surface: A disgusting news piece written about someone's uncle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article on uncle' means the article is placed after the uncle, so the order is reversed from the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something foul is dirty or impure, a straightforward adjective synonym.

clue.text: Blossom to see back in fairground

indicators.note: going back means reading the word from its end to its start
in means placed inside the following word

parts.note: only the first part, fair, is taken as written; the rest of the word is the mixing signal
taken as written

explanation.surface: Flowers you might go back to admire at a funfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairground' must be split: fair holds the reversed word, and ground, meaning crushed, tells you to mix all the letters up.
explanation.definitionFit: The freesia is a fragrant flowering plant, so blossom is a general term for this specific flower.

clue.text: Founder said to be in Unison

indicators.note: said tells us the word is spoken, so it matches by sound not spelling

parts.note: to founder is to sink, as a ship does

explanation.surface: A trade union's founding member is reported to belong to Unison, the UK public-service union.
explanation.walkthrough: Unison is capitalised to look like the British trade union; it means agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in sync means moving together in agreement, exactly as being in unison does.

clue.text: New handler due, may arrive without warning

indicators.note: something new is a fresh version, so these letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A replacement trainer expected soon could turn up with no notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unannounced comes with no herald or forewarning, so it happens without warning.

clue.text: Boring Edward promises to pay

parts.note: Ted is a short form of Edward
IOUs are written promises to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A dull man named Edward writes out notes saying he owes money.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious is dull and wearisome, which is a direct synonym for boring.

clue.text: Arranged to let me have English dish

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone has fixed it so they may eat a traditional English meal.
explanation.definitionFit: An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs cooked in a pan, so dish is a general category for it.

clue.text: Somerset village's dairy produce

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the village in Somerset, a county in south-west England, famous for its gorge
second meaning: the hard cheese named after that village

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes the cheese belong to the village it is named from.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheese originated in the Somerset village and still carries its name, so the place and the produce share it.

clue.text: Article by journalist describing place supported by pillars

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective used of such a place

parts.note: a column is a regular newspaper article
ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist; 'by' places it next to the first piece

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece by a reporter about a building held up on supports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' here is a newspaper column, not a grammatical a or the.
explanation.definitionFit: A building with columns, the adjective form, is one held up by pillars, since column and pillar are synonyms.

clue.text: Outlines retrospective charge on mixed gins

indicators.note: retrospective means looking backwards, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: a ward is someone in another's charge

indicators.note: mixed means jumbled together, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A backdated bar bill added for a round of assorted gins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like a fee; it is a person in someone's care.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawings are sketches showing the shapes of things, which is what outlines are.

clue.text: Blue vernal arrangement susceptible to damage

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things into a new order, here the letters of the preceding words

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A display of blue spring flowers is fragile and easily spoiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Being open to harm or attack is the core meaning of the adjective, so it matches susceptible to damage.

clue.text: Military unit that could be foreign or British

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large body of soldiers, as in a Roman army

definitions.text: that could be foreign or British
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word completing the French Foreign ... and the Royal British ..., a UK veterans' charity

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a fill-in: the answer follows either Foreign or British in a familiar name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman army division of several thousand soldiers is the original military sense of the word.

clue.text: Smart statue broken

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into pieces that can be reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An elegant sculpture has been smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' reads as stylish describing the statue; it means clever.
explanation.definitionFit: Astute means shrewd and quick-witted, matching the clever sense of smart.

clue.text: This android's a tad backward

indicators.note: backward means facing the other way, so the words are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A robot is described as slightly slow-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition names a character: Data is the android officer in Star Trek: The Next Generation.
explanation.definitionFit: Data is the name of the famous android crew member on the starship Enterprise in Star Trek.

clue.text: Disregard if caught in gentle disorder

indicators.note: something caught in is trapped inside, so it goes within the other letters
in disorder means jumbled, so these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Pay no attention if you are trapped in mild confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' does double duty: it supplies C and tells you to put it inside the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect something is to ignore or fail to attend to it, a verb synonym of disregard.

clue.text: In time for Christmas, Tiffany gets a dog

indicators.note: In tells us the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A girl called Tiffany receives a puppy just in time for the holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In time' reads as punctuality; only In is the instruction to look inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A mastiff is a large, powerful breed of guard dog, so it is one example of a dog.

clue.text: False shame, lacking energy

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so the named letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Pretended embarrassment that has no real feeling behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sham thing is fake or counterfeit, so as an adjective it means false.

clue.text: Son — and Henry, too — retreating from fire

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: retreating means moving backwards, so the last word is read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A father's boy and Henry both pulling back from a blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' looks like flames, but it is the verb meaning to discharge a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire a gun is to shoot it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Strangely, these absorb gang by a river

indicators.note: to absorb is to take in, so one piece goes inside the other
strangely means in an odd way, so these letters take an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Oddly, these people take in a group of friends beside a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ganges is the great sacred river of northern India, so it is one example of a river.
